Commentator: Brahmayogin (also known as Śrī Upaniṣad Brahmayogin) Editor: Śāstrī Mahādeva

The Yoga-tattva Upaniṣad.
Peace: "May He protect us both"—thus the peace mantra.
Inquiry into the Eightfold Yoga.
I shall proclaim the reality of yoga out of a desire for the welfare of yogins;
by hearing and by reciting it, one is liberated from all sins. (1)
The great yogi named Viṣṇu, a great being of great asceticism, is seen as the Supreme Person upon the path of reality, like a lamp. || 2 ||
Having propitiated the Lord of the World and prostrated before Him, the Grandfather (Brahmā) asked:
"Tell me the essence of Yoga, endowed with its eight limbs."
I worship that state of Rāmacandra, the Vaiṣṇava essence of yoga, by whose grace arise spiritual insight, mastery of yoga, and final liberation.

Indeed, this *Yogatattvopaniṣad*, which is a division of the *Kṛṣṇayajurveda*, shines forth as it culminates solely in Brahman; it is distinguished by mantra-laya and rājayoga, and is endowed with the stages of the beginning, the pot, familiarity, completion, and the state of the shrine. Herein, a brief [account] of this Upaniṣad...

The commentary is now commenced. The narrative concerning Brahmā and Viṣṇu as the agents of creation and maintenance is intended for the glorification of the knowledge [of Yoga]. First, the fruit of hearing and reciting this *Yogatattvopaniṣad*, which is about to be explained, [is stated].
(p. 364) He reveals [the title]: "The Yoga-tattva. Yoga is the *tattva* (reality) of the inner (*pratyak*) and the outer (*para*).

That Upaniṣad in which that which is to be propounded—the non-dual Brahman alone, devoid of the distinction between inner and outer and incapable of being divided, and free from any counter-correlate—is set forth, is this very *Yogatattvopaniṣad*. Merely by hearing and reading it...

The meaning is that there occurs a cessation of all sins. (1) He clarifies the true nature of this Vidyā-teacher [the Guru] with the words "Viṣṇu": on the path of the yoga of the knowledge of reality, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, is seen—that is, he is directly realized—just as a lamp is by yogis. (2) Him...
He says "him" (tam) because Brahmā asks [this question]. || 3 ||
Hṛṣīkeśa spoke to him regarding the rarity of the reality of yoga: "I shall speak; listen to it according to the truth.
All living beings are enveloped by the net of māyā through pleasures and pains. (4)
It is the path that brings liberation to them, which cuts through the net of illusion,
destroys birth, death, old age, and disease, and leads to deliverance.
The supreme state of absolute liberation is difficult to attain through various paths;
people have fallen into the snares of scriptures, being deluded by their own intellect.
That state which is inexpressible cannot be described even by those gods;
since it is of the nature of self-luminous manifestation, what need is there for a scripture to reveal it? (7)
Thus questioned, the Blessed One gave the answer to the question, beginning with the word "that" (*tam*).

He states that the secret meaning of what he himself must proclaim is difficult to attain even for those who possess various paths, ornaments, diverse scriptures, and their respective founders—beginning with the words "all" (*sarve*). They are "enveloped by the net of illusion," meaning by the cloths of illusion and its effects.

The meaning is that they are "obstructed" (āvṛtāḥ). (4–5) Since the path to liberation (kaivalya) is difficult to attain through means other than knowledge, according to the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which states, "There is no other path for going," [the author] says "they have fallen" (*patitāḥ*) to express that what is being spoken by me cannot be told by those deluded by the web of scriptures. By that—
And they are deluded by their own ignorance. (6) That by which everything from the sun to a pot is illuminated,
and by which the Vedas and scriptures become meaningful— that [Brahman] can never be an object of illumination by any scripture, because Brahman is solely self-luminous.
Because the meaning of the words and sentences is confused. || 7 ||
The very nature of the Supreme is partless, stainless, peaceful, transcending all, and free from affliction;
yet that same [nature], through the form of the individual soul (jīva), is enveloped by the fruits of merit and demerit.
How did that eternal state of the Supreme Self,
which transcends all states of being, consists of the nature of knowledge, and is stainless, come to belong to living beings?
In that [state], which vibrated like water, the sense of "I" (ahaṃkṛti) arose;
it became a body consisting of five elements, bound by the [gross] constituents and composed of the [three] qualities.

Regard that which is joined with pleasure and pain as the "living being" (jīva) through the contemplation of the living being; by that [designation], the name "living being" is applied to the pure Supreme Self.

Anticipating the objection that the individual soul (jīva) is distinct from the Supreme, he states—“niṣkalam” (partless)—that it is that very same [Supreme] which, being devoid of attributes, appears as if it were attaining the state of an individual soul. He raises an objection: “How can that [which is partless] deserve to be an individual soul? He provides the answer to this question: “sarva-” (all). In reality, it is Brahman.
It transcends the state of all phenomena. Any entity external to itself does not exist at all, being like the horn of a hare.
If it were to appear through the vision of one ignorant of oneself, then through the vision of one who knows oneself, it transcends the state of all phenomena;
its nature is knowledge because it is pure consciousness alone, meaning it is stainless and unattached to everything.
9. Regarding that which remains as its own nature alone, it is said that the one ignorant of itself superimposes upon it something other than itself:

"Like water stirred by a gentle breeze, there arises within that [state] the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*), which is denoted by the term 'Root Nature' (*mūlaprakṛti*) and consists of the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇas*). From that [arise] the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*); from those..."

From the five great elements that have been quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta), there arose a body composed of the seven constituents (dhātu), consisting of the three qualities (guṇa) and the five elements. Therein lies that consciousness which is joined with pleasure and pain.

Perform [this] with the contemplation of the individual soul (jīva). Therefore, within the Supreme Self—which is pure and transcends all states of being—the designation "individual soul" is said to belong to the non-dual Brahman itself through its association with the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti). || 11 ||
For the individual soul (jīva) who is divested of natural qualities, there is the state of being the Supreme Self;
yet [in its unliberated state], there are desire, anger, fear, as well as delusion, greed, pride, and passion (rajas); birth and death, wretchedness, grief, drowsiness, hunger, and thirst. (12)
Thirst, shame, fear, suffering, despondency, and even joy—one who is completely liberated from these defects is considered a solitary soul (kevala). || 13 ||
When one becomes free from the qualities of material nature (*prākṛtaguṇa*), then the individual soul (*jīva*) itself becomes the absolute Supreme Self (*kevalaparamātman*);
thus it is said: "desire," etc. Here, the change in gender and number is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
12. The simultaneous practice of knowledge (*jñāna*) and yoga (*yoga*).
Therefore, for the sake of destroying these defects, I shall tell you the means:
how can knowledge devoid of yoga certainly bestow liberation? (14)
Even yoga, if devoid of knowledge, is not capable of accomplishing the work of liberation;
therefore, one who desires liberation should practice both knowledge and yoga with firm resolve. (15)

Since this is so, therefore: although pure, attributeless knowledge (*nirviśeṣajñāna*) bestows liberation, the absence of that [liberation] in the case of knowledge with attributes (*saviśeṣajñāna*) implies a longing for yoga.
Thus, he says "yoga-less" (verse 14) to indicate that one should practice both knowledge and yoga simultaneously. Since this is so, therefore (verse 15).
From ignorance alone arises the cycle of worldly existence, and through knowledge alone one is liberated.
At the very beginning, that which is the nature of knowledge is itself knowledge, the sole means for realizing the object of knowledge.

By whom one's own nature has been known—that which is absolute liberation, the supreme state, partless, stainless, directly manifest, and consisting of the form of existence, consciousness, and bliss. (17)
That which is devoid of the knowledge of arising, persistence, dissolution, and manifestation—this is declared to be "knowledge. Now, I shall speak to you of yoga. 18.

He states that the causes of bondage and liberation are one's own ignorance and one's own knowledge, saying "from ignorance" (ajñānāt). Regarding that, he explains what kind of knowledge it is, saying "knowledge" (jñāna). [Verses 16–17] That which is devoid of such knowledge is the manifestation that "this has arisen, exists, and is withdrawn as something separate from oneself."

That alone is declared to be non-differentiated knowledge (*nirviśeṣa-jñāna*). Indeed, it does not depend upon means such as yoga for the attainment of its own fruit. However, that differentiated knowledge (*saviśeṣa-jñāna*) which has the lower Brahman as its object depends upon yoga for the sake of pacifying the distinctions inherent within itself. [This is] by means of differentiated knowledge.
He says "Now" (*atha*) to state that which he intends to collect [and explain]:
the meaning is, "Now, after the arising of knowledge characterized by distinctions, listen to the yoga that is the cause for its becoming free from distinctions."
Yoga is fourfold, beginning with Mantra-yoga; for indeed, O Brahmin, yoga is divided in many ways according to conventional usage:
Mantra-yoga, Laya-yoga, Haṭha-yoga, and Rāja-yoga. (19)

When the question arises as to what kind of yoga this is, he says "Yoga, indeed... to show that although ultimate yoga is one, it is divided into many types due to the variety of its means. To the question "How is that so?", he replies "By mantra. Thus, there are four primary yogas. || 19 ||
The stages of yoga, beginning with *ārambha*, are as follows:
*ārambha*, *ghaṭa*, and likewise *paricaya* are recorded;
and the stage of *niṣpatti* is proclaimed everywhere. (20)
The auxiliary practices (aṅgayoga), however, are: and "commencement" (ārambha). || 20 ||
(368) O Brahmin, I shall describe the characteristics of these [practices], specifically the characteristics of mantra-yoga; listen briefly.
He who recites a mantra joined with the *mātṛkā* for twelve years [attains success]. || 21 ||
Gradually one attains knowledge endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest;
yet the lowest of practitioners, being of little intelligence, pursues this yoga.
These are the words of the Sūtra; regarding them, first of all, out of compassion for those of dull intellect, he explains the application of mantra, beginning with the word "mātṛkā" (21–22).
The characteristic of Layayoga:
Layayoga is said to be the dissolution of the mind in millions of ways;
whether walking, standing, sleeping, or eating, one should meditate upon the partless Lord. (23)
That indeed is *layayoga*; now hear the doctrine of *ghaṭhayoga*.
He describes the method of *layayoga* with the words "laya" etc.; therein, this most essential [state] proceeds. (23)
The limbs of Haṭhayoga are indeed yama, niyama, āsana, and prāṇasaṃyama. || 24 ||
Withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation on Hari between the eyebrows, and samādhi as the state of equanimity—this is called the eight-limbed yoga. (25)
Mahāmudrā, Mahābandha, Mahāvedha, and Khecarī; likewise Jālandhara, Uḍḍiyāṇa, and Mūlabandha. (26)
The prolonged concentration on the *praṇava*, as well as listening to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), and *vajrolī*, *amarolī*, and *sahajolī*—these are considered the threefold [yogas]. (27)
He describes Haṭhayoga distinguished by eight limbs—beginning with "Haṭha" (verses 24–25). Again, he explains the twelve-limbed yoga—beginning with "Mahāmudrā" (verses 26–27).
O Brahmin, hear now the characteristics of these principal limbs—yama, niyama, and āsana—in their true essence, one by one.
Among the yamas, moderation in diet (laghvāhāra) alone is primary; no other is so. (28)

O Four-faced One, non-violence alone is indeed the foremost among the observances (niyamas). Furthermore, there is a fourfold [classification] consisting of the Siddha, Padma, Siṃha, and Bhadra [postures]. || 29 ||
In total, this yoga is distinguished by twenty limbs.

He states the individual definitions of these limbs with the words "of these. Among the ten restraints (*yama*), he states the primary means [to success] with the word "light" (*laghu*). Likewise, among the ten observances (*niyama*)...
He states the primary means [of practice] as "non-violence" (ahiṃsā) and so forth. Postures (āsanas) are infinite; among them, eighty postures are primary.
Even among those, he says that the fourfold group of postures beginning with Siddha is the most important:
"Siddha," etc. (verse 29).
The abandonment of obstacles to the practice of yoga:
O Four-faced One, at the time of initial practice, there may arise obstacles such as laziness, boastfulness, the company of rogues, and the pursuit of mantras and other such means. (30)
Having understood that the desire for minerals, women, and other such things are indeed composed of a mirage, the wise man should abandon all obstacles through the power of his merit. || 31 ||
He says that one should abandon the web of obstacles that arises during the time of practicing yoga: "First...
(p. 370). Regarding the nature of the hut and the seat appropriate for breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should then perform breath control oneself while seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*).
One should construct a very beautiful monastery with a narrow door that is free from any cracks.
It should be carefully smeared with cow dung or whitewash,
and it must be diligently cleared of bedbugs, mosquitoes, and bats.
And day by day it was especially swept clean with a broom,
perfumed with fragrant scents, and incensed with guggulu and other aromatics.
Neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass;
having sat there, the wise man should assume the lotus posture (padmāsana). || 35 ||
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "prāṇāyāmam" (breath control). He describes the characteristics of the hut suitable for breath control: "suśobhanam" (very beautiful). || 32–34 ||
He states the characteristics of the yogin: "In that regard" (tatra). || 35 ||
The method for beginning *prāṇāyāma*:
With the body straight and palms joined in reverence, one should bow to one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
Then, with the thumb of the right hand alone, [one should block] the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī]. (36)
Having restrained [the breath], one should fill the air through the *iḍā* very slowly;
according to one's capacity and without conflict, one should then perform the *kumbhaka*.
Again, one should exhale through the Piṅgalā very slowly and not with force;
then, having filled [the breath] through the Piṅgalā, one should fill the abdomen slowly.
Having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, one should exhale slowly through the iḍā;
having filled it with that same [nostril] through which one would exhale, one should retain it without conflict. (39)
One should prostrate at the time of beginning yoga. To the question "What then?
he states the sequence for the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the word "tataḥ" (then). || 36-39 ||

Prāṇāyāma is preceded by a regulation of the *mātrās*. Having circumambulated the knee neither too quickly nor too slowly, one should perform the snapping of the fingers; that is proclaimed as a *mātrā*. (40)
Having filled the breath through the *iḍā* [left nostril] slowly with sixteen measures (*mātrā*),
one should then retain the filled air for sixty-four measures.
One should again recite [the mantra] through the piṅgalā-nāḍī for thirty-two mātrās;
then, having filled [it] through the piṅgalā as before, one should remain well-composed.
One should practice breath-retentions (kumbhaka) four times a day— at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight— gradually increasing up to eighty repetitions each time.
Having stated the definition of general *prāṇāyāma*, he now states the definition of specific *prāṇāyāma* by first demonstrating the measurement of its duration—
beginning with the words "jānu" (verse 40–42). He states the limit of the number of times *prāṇāyāma* should be performed each day:
"In the morning," [so it is said]. || 43 ||
The intermediate result is the purification of the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*) and its signs.
Thus, from three months of practice, the purification of the channels occurs;
when the purification of the channels has taken place, then the signs appear externally. (44)
(372) Those [signs] arise within the body of the yogin; I shall describe them in their entirety:
lightness of the body, radiance, and the increase of the digestive fire. (45)
"And at that time, emaciation of the body will certainly arise.

He states the intermediate result of such practice with the word "evam" (thus). To the question, "What are the signs of the purification of the channels? he replies with the verse beginning "yadā" (when). (Verses 44–48)
Regarding the regulation of food and other factors during the time of practicing yoga:
the best among those who know yoga should avoid food that creates obstacles to yoga. (46)
Salt, mustard, sour, hot, dry, and pungent;
various leafy vegetables such as asafoetida and the like; and the frequenting of fire, women, and roads—[these are to be avoided]. (47)
One should avoid physical hardships such as bathing at dawn or fasting;
at the beginning of the practice, a diet of milk and ghee is recommended. (48)
They know that wheat, mung beans, and rice increase the power of yoga;
thereafter, through the mastery of the kumbhaka alone, one becomes capable of retaining the vital air for as long as desired.

By retaining the breath according to one's desire, the *kevala-kumbhaka* (absolute retention) is accomplished; when the *kevala-kumbhaka*, devoid of exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), has been mastered. || 50 ||

"Nothing whatsoever is difficult for him to obtain within the three worlds. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "From that... (verse 49). To the question "What would happen because of that?", he says: "As desired... (verse 50).
(373) The supernatural powers such as perspiration:
first, perspiration arises; therefore, one should perform massage with it. || 51 ||
Furthermore, from the gradual and steady practice of breath-retention (dhāraṇā), trembling occurs in the body of the embodied being who remains seated in the posture. || 52 ||
From practice even more intense than that, the state of *dardara* arises by itself;
and when the state of *dardara* proceeds by leaping up again and again, || 53 ||
The yogi seated in the lotus posture moves along the ground in that manner;
then, through even more advanced practice, the leaving of the earth occurs.
Remaining in the lotus posture (padmāsana), he departs, leaving the earth behind;
likewise, superhuman activities and such powers arise.
He should not display his power, nor should he show an excessive exertion;
whether the suffering be slight or manifold, the yogi is then not distressed.
There is little urine and feces, and one experiences very little sleep;
there is nasal mucus, eye-secretion, saliva, and a foul odor of sweat on the face. (57)
Beyond that, none of these arise for him in any way whatsoever;
from even greater practice than that, great power is produced. (58)
By means of which one may attain the power of moving on the earth and be capable of conquering those who move on the earth—whether it be a tiger, a *śarabha*, an elephant, or even a *gavaya*. (59)
Or like a lion, they are killed by that yogi when struck by his hand;
for the form of the yogi may even be like that of Kaṃdarpa. (60)
Women, being under the sway of that form, long for union with him;
if he were to engage in union, his seminal essence would be lost. (61)
Having avoided attachment to women, one should practice with diligence;
by the retention of the *bindu*, a sweet fragrance arises upon the body of the yogin. (62)
From the practice of one-quarter, one-half, three-quarters, and full [breath retention], there arise perspiration and so forth, ending with superhuman feats.
From the one-quarter breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), perspiration occurs even when encountering suffering. (Sūtras 51–56)

He states that for the yogin practicing in this manner, there arises great strength, beauty, aversion toward women and the like, and a divine fragrance from his own limbs, preceded by the absence of human deformities—
beginning with the words "alpa" (small). Those which bind the joints and ligaments produced from one's own body are called *kīlavas*.

The bindings of the vital airs (*vāyubandha*). It vitiates the body and produces a state of emaciation; thus it is *dūṣikā*, such as consumption (*kṣaya*) and so forth, or the impurity of the eyes. The remainder is clear. || 57 || Furthermore—“therefrom” || 58 || How is that? “Like a tiger” || 59–62 ||
The recitation of the *praṇava* is for the sake of destroying obstacles to yoga; this is the stage of commencement.
Then, seated in a secluded place, one should recite the *praṇava* with the *pluta* (protracted) measure for the purpose of destroying previously accumulated sins. (63)
The Praṇava is the mantra that removes all obstacles and destroys all defects;
through such practice and yoga, perfection arises from the very beginning. 64.

(375) He says "then" (tataḥ) [in verse 63] to mean that if yoga is not accomplished due to the influence of obstacles, then the recitation of the *praṇava* should be performed for their pacification. He says "thus" (evam) [in verse 64] to indicate that this undertaking is begun because the attainment of signs such as perspiration and pleasant fragrance has been initiated.
From that, the state of the jar (ghaṭāvasthā) arises; the state of the jar is intent upon the practice of breath-control (pavana).
Prāṇa, apāna, mind, and intellect [are the means] for the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). || 65 ||
When they attain unity through mutual non-contradiction, that is called the state of the jar (ghaṭāvasthā); I shall now describe its characteristics. || 66 ||
One should adopt a quarter-part of the practice previously described;
one should practice it at a single session, either by day or in the evening. (67)
One should perform the *kevala-kumbhaka* once every day.
He describes the *ghaṭa-yoga* with the words "tataḥ" (then), etc. (vv. 65–67).
The definition of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is the clear drawing back of the senses from their respective objects. 68.
The yogi, having established himself in *kumbhaka*, that is called *pratyāhāra*.
He states the essential nature of *pratyāhāra* with the words "the senses," etc. (68).
Whatever form one perceives with the eyes through the nature of concentration (dhāraṇā), one should contemplate that very thing as the Self. || 69 ||
Whatever one hears with the two ears, one should contemplate that as the Self; whatever one perceives with the nose, one should contemplate that as the Self. (70)
Whatever taste the tongue eats, the yogi should contemplate that as the Self;
whatever the skin touches, the yogi should contemplate that as the Self. (71)
In this manner, one should fix the organs of knowledge (jñānendriyas) each upon their respective self. He states the definition of *dhāraṇā* [as follows]: "Whatever... (verses 69–71).

The meaning is that the collection of sense organs such as the eye and their corresponding objects, which were conceptualized as non-Brahman during the state of one's own ignorance, should be realized as Brahman within the inner self (pratīc) during the state of one's own knowledge.
The accomplishments of the dhāraṇās and the method for their concealment [are taught];
the yogi, free from sloth, should practice with effort every day for the duration of one watch (yāma). || 72 ||
Or just as the power of the mind certainly arises for the yogin—such as hearing from afar, seeing from afar, and likewise traveling to a distance in an instant. (73)
There is the perfection of speech, the ability to assume any form at will, and likewise the power of invisibility;
furthermore, by anointing with [the mixture of] feces and urine, iron and other metals turn into gold. (74)
Through the practice of constant repetition, his movement shall become like that of the sky;
therefore, for the sake of attaining yoga, the wise yogi should always remain mindful.
These are the obstacles to great accomplishment; a wise man should not take delight in them.
A king among yogis should not display his own power to just anyone.
Just as one who is deluded, just as one who is foolish, or just as one who is deaf, so should he conduct himself toward the world for the sake of protecting his own power. (77)
The disciples, moreover, will undoubtedly entreat him for their respective tasks; thus, preoccupied with those various duties, he will forget his own spiritual practice. (78)
Having abandoned all worldly activities, the ascetic should be devoted to yoga;
without forgetting the words of the guru, he should practice them day and night. (79)
In this way, the state of the jar may arise through the yoga of continuous practice;
however, for one who lacks such practice, it is not accomplished through idle conversation.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always practice yoga alone.
To the question, "What arises from that? he says: "For only a watch [of the day]," etc. (72). What is that?
"Hearing from afar," etc. (73–75). Because the manifestation of one's own supernatural powers becomes an obstacle to further yoga.
Therefore, disregarding the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and concealing one's own capacity, one should practice yoga alone;

thus he says: "These... (vv. 76–77). One becomes preoccupied with performing various actions, meaning the mind is distracted by the performance of those various tasks. Consequently, [one fails] in one's own practice (vv. 78–79). It is through practice alone that this [attainment occurs].
He says "thus" (evam) [in verse 80] to show that the state of being a jar is established in no other way.
Then, from that, the stage of proficiency arises through the practice of yoga. || 81 ||
The vital air, having been thoroughly mastered through effort together with the fire,
should enter the Suṣumnā after having visualized the Kuṇḍalinī, without obstruction.
The mind, together with the vital air, should enter the great path;
for one whose mind and breath enter the *suṣumnā* here in this world. (83)
He states the nature of familiarity [with the breath] with the words "from that" (tataḥ). How so? With the words "the wind" (vāyuḥ).
The "great path" means the gateway of the *suṣumnā*; likewise, this is called the state of familiarization (*paricaya-avasthā*).

(378) Within the maṇḍalas of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and space—there are the five *dhāraṇās* of the Brahmās. In these five, the *dhāraṇā* of the deities is said to be fivefold. (84)
The region from the feet up to the knees is said to be the locus of earth;
the earth is square, yellow in color, and has the syllable *la*. (85)
Having ascended the wind upon the earth and joined it with the letter *la*, one should meditate on [the deity] in the form of four arms, with four faces, and golden in color. (86)
If one retains [the breath] for five ghaṭikās, one attains victory over the earth;
through union with the earth, death shall not occur for this yogin. (87)
The region from the navel down to the anus is proclaimed to be the abode of the waters (Ap).
Water is described as being half-moon-shaped, white, and having the seed-syllable "vaṃ. || 88 ||
Having ascended Vāyu in the western quarter, accompanied by the syllable *va*,
one should remember the god Nārāyaṇa, who has four arms and wears a crown.
One who meditates for five ghaṭikās upon Acyuta, who resembles pure crystal and is clad in yellow garments, is liberated from all sins. || 90 ||
From that water there is no fear; death does not exist within the water.
From the anus up to the heart, the region of fire is proclaimed. (91)
Fire is a red triangle, originating from the syllable *ra*;
having superimposed wind upon fire, it blazes forth from the syllable *ra*.
Meditating upon Rudra, who has three eyes, bestows boons, resembles the rising sun, has all his limbs smeared with ashes, and is exceedingly gracious; (93)
If one maintains this for five ghaṭikās, one is not burned by fire;
nor is the body burned even when one has entered a pit of fire.
From the heart to the middle of the eyebrows, the locus of Vāyu is proclaimed;
it is a black six-cornered figure, radiant with the syllable Ya. (95)
One should meditate upon the Wind-god in the station of the Maruts, radiant with the syllable *ya*, and there [one should meditate upon] the omniscient Lord, whose face is everywhere. 96.
If one should hold [the breath] for five ghaṭikās, one becomes like the wind moving through space;
for the yogin, there is no death, nor does fear of the wind arise.
From the midpoint of the eyebrows up to the crown of the head is said to be the location of space (ākāśa).
It is the sphere of the void, smoky in color, and radiant with the syllable *ha*.
Having superimposed the wind upon the ether, one should place Śaṅkara above the letter *ha*—the Great God in the form of the *bindu*, Sadāśiva whose form is the void. || 99 ||
Resembling pure crystal, with the young moon as his crest-jewel, endowed with five faces, gentle, possessing ten arms and three eyes. 100.
He who maintains his form with all weapons, adorned with all ornaments, whose body is half Umā, the granter of boons, the cause of all causes. (101)
By means of the retention of space, his power of moving through the sky (khecaratva) will certainly arise;
wherever he may be situated, he experiences supreme happiness.
In this manner, the wise yogi should perform the five *dhāraṇās*;
then his body shall become firm, and death shall not exist for him. (103)
The one of great intelligence does not perish even by the dissolution of Brahmā.

Therefore, he describes the fivefold meditation on Brahmā (*pañcabrahmadhāraṇā*) within the sphere of the five elements divided according to their own constituent parts, beginning with the word "Earth" (*bhūmi*). Of the gods...

[This concerns] those beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva. || 84 || Regarding that, first [is the section] beginning with "from the feet. By the word "earth" (pṛthivī), the earthly sphere (pārthivamaṇḍala) is meant. || 85 || Then, regarding the earthly [sphere], || 86–87 || he states the meditation on Viṣṇu and its fruit within this earthly sphere: "up to the knees," etc. || 88–90 || [Now, regarding] the fire sphere (vahnimaṇḍala):

He describes the meditation on Rudra and its fruit with the words "From the anus... (verses 91–94). He describes the meditation on Īśvara within the sphere of air and its fruit with the words "From the heart... (verses 95–97).

He describes the meditation on Sadāśiva within the sphere of space and its fruit: "One should practice that meditation with attributes from the middle of the eyebrows upwards, for exactly sixty ghaṭikās. (104)

"Having restrained the vital air in the ether [of the heart], one should meditate on the deity who grants desired boons"—this is meditation with attributes (*saguṇa-dhyāna*), which bestows qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
He describes the two types of meditation according to the distinction between those with attributes and those without: "one should practice... [and so forth].
From meditation on the attributeless, there is the perfection of samādhi;
and for one engaged in meditation on the attributeless, samādhi arises from that. || 105 ||
In just twelve days, the wise man shall attain samādhi; by restraining the vital breath (vāyu), he becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). 106.

Samādhi is the state of equality between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). The meaning is that samādhi is abiding in one's own true nature, [realizing] that nothing exists apart from Brahman. [This occurs] in such a manner within twelve days alone. || 105-106 ||

He explains the term *samādhi*: "It is *samādhi*. The meaning is that *samādhi* is precisely the state of equality between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) in their implied sense (*lakṣyarūpa*), preceded by the abandonment of the disparity between their literal meanings (*vācyārtha*).
For one who has attained perfection in yoga, the relinquishing or non-relinquishing of the body occurs according to his own will; if he desires to cast off his own body, he may do so by himself.
He should merge into the Supreme Brahman; for him, no further departure [of the soul] is intended.
However, if he does not wish to relinquish his own dear body, [he may depart]. 108.
Wandering through all the worlds, endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest,
the god sometimes becomes [a deity] by his own will and is honored in heaven.
Whether a human or a yakṣa, one may become [anything] in an instant by one's own will;
by one's own will, one may become a lion, a tiger, an elephant, or a horse, and attain multiplicity.
The yogin may act exactly as he pleases, or like Maheśvara himself;
for while there is a difference due to the distinction in practice, the fruit is indeed the same.

The yogin who considers that the three bodies exist even as a manifestation distinct from his own self, having abandoned them, merges into the Supreme Brahman. If, however, he does not wish to abandon them in this way, manifesting his manifold powers, he may wander in this world until the dissolution of all beings; thus it is said: "If... (verse 107).
The meaning is that the primary fruit, which is liberation (kaivalya), is indeed equal [in both cases]. || 111 ||
The characteristic of the Great Bond (*mahābandha*):
one should place the heel of the left foot at the site of the *yoni*.
Having extended the right leg, one should hold it firmly with both hands. (112)
Placing the chin upon the heart, one should again fill [the body] with air;
having retained it through kumbhaka according to one's capacity, one should then exhale.
Having practiced with the left limb, one should practice with the right limb;
whichever foot is extended, one should place it upon the thigh.
This indeed is the Great Lock (Mahābandha); one should practice it thus in both [postures].
The characteristics of Mahāmudrā are recorded elsewhere: "With the shanks placed upon the chest, one should press the opening of the vulva with the left foot."
Holding the outstretched right foot with both hands,
and filling the two cavities of the abdomen with breath, one should hold it fixed at the crown of the head;
this is indeed declared to be the Mahāmudrā for men, which destroys all sins.

Thus [it is said]. He states the definition of the "Great Bond" (mahābandha): "the heel," etc. (verses 112–113). "One should honor," "offer," or "place upon"—this is the meaning (verse 114). "One should practice" means that it should be done on the right side just as it was on the left side.
The characteristic of the Great Piercing:
the yogi, established in the Great Lock (mahābandha) and single-minded, should perform the inhalation (pūraka). 115.
Having restrained the movement of the winds by means of the silent throat-seal (kaṇṭhamudrā) and having firmly pressed both nostrils, the wind vibrates swiftly.
This very *mahāvedha* is practiced incessantly by the perfected ones (*siddhas*).
[The author] states the nature of this *vedha* in the verse beginning with "the great bandha" (*mahābandha*) || 115 ||
Having obstructed— that is, covered— the movement of the winds of exhalation, inhalation, recaka,
and pūraka by means of the throat-mudrā and the Jālandhara-bandha, the prāṇa-vāyu then thoroughly overcomes and transcends both the iḍā and piṅgalā channels, and swiftly enters the suṣumnā.
"That which throbbs" refers to this very [state]. || 116 ||
One should hold the tongue, having turned it back, within the hollow of the skull; this is the true nature of Khecarī. || 117 ||
This gaze fixed between the eyebrows is also the *mudrā* known as *khecarī*.
He describes the essential nature of *khecarī*: "Internally," etc. (117).
Regarding the nature of the three bandhas and their fruit:
contracting the throat, one should fix [the breath] at the heart with a firm mind. (118)
This is the lock known as Jālandhara, the lion to the elephant of death;
it is the lock by which the vital breath is made to soar upward into the Suṣumnā. (119)
This binding known as Uḍḍiyāṇa has indeed been proclaimed by the yogis:
one should firmly contract [the perineum] while pressing the perineal region with the heel. 120.
Having raised the apāna upward, this is called the yonibandha;
by means of the mūlabandha, prāṇa and apāna, as well as nāda and bindu, attain oneness.
Having attained the perfection of yoga, it bestows [the fruits]; there is no doubt in this matter.
He describes the nature of the three bonds and their results, beginning with the words "the throat" (kaṇṭham), etc. (vv. 118–121).
The characteristic of that which effects the reversal, and its fruit:
the "effecting" [practice] is called "reversal," and it destroys all mental and physical ailments. || 122 ||
For the practitioner who is constantly engaged in practice, large quantities of food that increase the digestive fire should be provided. 123.
If the digestive fire becomes weak due to insufficient food, it may destroy the body in an instant;
therefore, on the first day, one should remain for a moment with the head downward and the feet upward.
If one practices for even slightly more than a moment day after day,
wrinkles and grey hair will no longer be seen after six months and a half.
He who practices this constantly for even a single watch (yāma) becomes a conqueror of time.
Regarding the "inversion" (viparītakaraṇī), he states its fruit as follows: "the inversion" (karaṇī). || 122-123 ||
It is called "the performer of the contrary" because it acts in a manner opposite to one's own natural state; he elaborates upon this very point with the verse beginning "Below."
The true nature of Vajroli:
he who practices Vajroli is a yogi who becomes a vessel for spiritual accomplishments. || 126 ||
If that very yoga-siddhi is obtained, it stands within one's hand;
one knows the past and the future, and khecarī certainly becomes [attained]. 127.
He describes the true nature of Vajroli and its fruit, beginning with the words "Vajroli. What indeed is Vajroli?
Having poured cow's milk into a bell-metal vessel, one swallows it by means of the penis, which is like the tube of the Vajroli, and then expels it again.

(p. 385) Having practiced the swallowing and so forth once more, one should emit semen into the circle of the woman's womb and swallow it together with her blood; this very practice is called *vajrolī*. He says that he who practices it becomes a perfected one (*siddha*), stating: "It is obtained. This yogi knows the past and the future. Of him alone...
He who daily drinks the *amarī* (the immortal fluid) which is the very nature of *amarolī*, and practices *nasya* day after day,
and constantly practices *vajrolī*, is said to be one who has mastered *amarolī*. (128)
He describes the nature of the *amarolī*: "The *amarī*," etc. By the word *amarī*, urine is meant.

Having set aside the first and last streams and taking the middle stream in his hand or in a vessel, that yogi who drinks one-third of it day after day and performs nasal drops (*nasya*) with it through both nostrils constantly—

"That which is called the practice of *vajrolī* is itself termed *amarolī*. And so it is stated in the *Haṭhayogatantra*: 'Because of the predominance of bile (*pitta*), one should [avoid] the first stream...'"
Having abandoned the final stream because it is devoid of essence,
the cool middle stream is cultivated by those perfected in the *vajrolī* for the sake of attaining the perfection of the *amarolī*.
Thus, that perfection which arises without the drinking of the *amarī* [nectar] by one who has attained the *amarolī* [attainment] is called *sahajolī*. || 128 ||
The perfection of Rājayoga then occurs; Rājayoga certainly does not arise otherwise.
When the practices have been perfected by yogins through Rājayoga, [then it is attained]. || 129 ||
Then, discernment and dispassion certainly arise for the yogin;
Viṣṇu by name is the great yogin, the great being, and the one of great austerity. || 130 ||
Just as a lamp is seen on the path of reality, so is Puruṣottama perceived. (p.
386) He states the true nature of Rājayoga with the word "tataḥ" (therefore): the meaning is that Rājayoga does not occur without the practice of Haṭha consisting of twenty components. || 129 ||

This Rājayoga is perfected through Haṭhayoga because it is the king of yogas. For it is there alone that the Blessed One is perceived; thus he says, "Viṣṇu. This is because the reality of Puruṣottama, which is free from the dualities of the perishable and the imperishable, is characterized solely by Rājayoga through the realization "I am He" (so 'ham asmi). || 130 ||
The determination of the cause of dispassion: He who, having squeezed that very breast which was formerly sucked, now experiences joy. (131)
Since she was born from the vulva and delights in that very same vulva,
she who is the mother is also the wife, and she who is the wife is indeed the mother.
He who was a father becomes again a son, and he who was a son becomes again a father;
thus, by means of the wheel of saṃsāra, they revolve like buckets on the wheel of a well.
Wandering through various wombs and births, one experiences the worlds upon hearing [the teaching].
This is traditionally taught for the sake of cultivating external detachment toward wives and other objects that exceed the state of being the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama):
"He who [drinks] from the breast," and so forth; the meaning is "toward such a person. In that very same kind of womb... [131] ...in that very same kind of womb.

Delighting in [this], one enjoys joy. Regarding the fact that she who is one’s mother in this birth becomes one’s wife in another existence, and she who is one’s wife becomes one’s very mother in another existence, he says: "She who is the mother...
The meaning is: she who is the mother remains the mother indeed. Thus... 132. In this manner...

Perceiving that there exists anything whatsoever apart from the reality of Puruṣottama, they wander like pots on a wheel within the cycle of existence, undergoing birth and death in various wombs. Therefore, having heard from the mouths of the Śruti and the Guru that "Brahman alone is all; there is nothing apart from Brahman," [one should realize this].
The seeker of liberation attains the highest worlds, which serve as the abodes of Brahmā and the other gods;
having dwelt there as long as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Brahman persists, they attain absolute liberation (kaivalya) along with Him.
(387) The meditation on the *praṇava* within the heart-lotus:
the three worlds, the three Vedas, the three twilights, and the three vowels. || 134 ||
The three fires and the three qualities are all established within the three syllables;
and he who studies even half a syllable of those three syllables [attains the goal]. (135)
By that all this is strung together; that is the Truth, that is the supreme state.
Just as fragrance is within the flower, and just as clarified butter is within the milk. || 136 ||
Just as oil exists within sesame seeds and gold within stones, so too the lotus is situated in the location of the heart; its face is turned downwards. (137)
With its stalk above and its drop below, the mind is situated in its center;
the lotus is exhaled by the syllable *A* and pierced by the syllable *U*.
In the letter *ma*, one attains the sound which is motionless for half a mora;
it resembles pure crystal, is partless, and destroys all evil. (139)
A person whose self is disciplined in yoga attains that supreme state.

As a means to that end, within the three-syllabled *praṇava*— which consists of the four measures (*mātrā*) such as the forms pertaining to the higher and lower Brahman— the three worlds beginning with Bhūḥ are sequentially [established].
The three Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda; the three twilight prayers (saṃdhyās) beginning with the morning twilight;
the three vowels distinguished as A, U, and M; the three fires distinguished as Gārhapatya and so forth;
and the three qualities (guṇas) beginning with Sattva—all these are "sthitāḥ," meaning they are established. || 134 ||

Through the oral instruction of the Śruti and the Guru, he understands the three syllables beginning with *a*, as well as the universe (*viśva*), the cosmic man (*virāj*), and the *otrā* state, which serve as the substrata for their superimposition. By that yogi who has attained the state of the Fourth (*turya*), all this collection of phenomenal expansion is perceived as woven together [with him], thinking: "I alone am all this."

"Pervaded" (vyāptam): that which is established by the negation of the state of being a pervader dependent upon a pervaded is the Truth (satyam). That which is mere existence (sattāmātra) is itself the supreme, unsurpassed "ground" (padam), because it is reached as its own remainder;
the meaning is that nothing but Brahman alone remains. But how [is this so] for the Fourth (turya)?
Regarding the state of being all-pervasive, he explains four illustrations with the verse beginning "puṣpa" (verse 136).

The meaning is as follows: just as gold exists pervading everything within a solid mass of gold ore without distinction, so too does [the Self] exist. Having thus described that pervasive consciousness, [the text now sets forth] its locus of perception, its essential nature, and the fruit of knowing it.

He clarifies this with the words "in the location of the heart" (*hṛdisthāne*). In the location of the heart, that is, in the region of the chest, there exists the heart-lotus (*hṛtpadma*), which has an upward stalk and a downward-facing mouth like a plantain flower.
Beneath that is the unmanifest space (*avyākṛtākāśa*) of the *bindu*. In its center is the mind (*manas*). || 137 ||
The inner consciousness (pratyak-caitanya) remains as the illuminator of the existence and non-existence of the thousands of modifications of that [mind].

To lead it upward, to cause it to expand, and to effect the direct realization of the consciousness residing therein, he states the means: "The letter A. When the consciousness of the Viśva-Virāj and the experiencer (otṛ) within the letter A is directly realized—

When the mind is present, the heart-lotus, being turned upward, becomes exhaled and rises; through the direct realization of the consciousness that is the witness—consisting of the syllable *U*, its presiding deity, the Taijasa-sūtra, and the Anujñātṛ—it is split open and attains expansion. || 138 ||

When the consciousness that is of one flavor with the permission (*anujñā*), the seed (*bīja*), the wisdom (*prājña*), and the individual witness (*adhyakṣa*)— all of which are characterized by the letter *M*— is directly realized, then the resonance of the *praṇava*, which consists of that very self, unfolds as the *nāda* of the Lord-principle (*īśvaratattva*). As for the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), it is the culmination of the expansion of the three measures beginning with the letter *A*.

When presided over by the non-conceptual state of the second and fourth [turiya], it becomes immovable. Therein, that which is perceived through continuous contemplation causes the web of merit and demerit to perish;
it resembles pure crystal, destroys sin, and is in reality partless and devoid of any counterpart.

That which remains as the Self alone— meaning that the person whose self is disciplined by the yoga described above attains that supreme state and becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.

The cessation of the activity of all the organs is the means for the realization of the Self; as a tortoise withdraws its own hands, feet, and head into itself, so [should one restrain the senses]. || 140 ||
Thus, when all the gates have been filled with air and expelled,
and the nine gates are closed, the breath is likewise exhaled upwards.
Just as a lamp within a jar is known as *kumbhaka* when in a windless place, so too [the breath] is held when the nine gates are closed in a secluded and undisturbed location. (142)
Through the practice of yoga, one is certain to remain as the Self alone.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

He states that the means for attaining that realization is indeed the cessation of all activity of the organs— using the word "tortoise": just as a tortoise remains like a stone by withdrawing its own limbs,
so too the yogi, having withdrawn [the breath] filled with air from all nine gates and from all the channels of the nerves.

He states that during the stages of inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*), there occurs an upward breath through the path of the *suṣumnā*, which is delimited by the hollows of the channels (*nāḍī*) filled and emptied by the air— expressed by the word "prohibited" (*niṣiddha*).
When the nine gates are prohibited, that is, restrained, then [the breath moves] from the eastern gate of the *suṣumnā*.

Having pierced that which resides in the *mūlādhāra*, the breath should then go upward; the meaning is that one should remain in the state of pure *kumbhaka* (retention), wherein the activity of exhalation has ceased. || 141 ||

He states the definition of *kumbhaka* [breath-retention] with the words "in the middle of the jar" (*ghaṭamadhye*). Thus, having realized the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) through the practice of pure *kumbhaka*, one becomes fulfilled; he concludes this with the words "by those that are prohibited" (*niṣiddhaiḥ*).
By the nine gates being closed—meaning prohibited from their respective functions—the yogi, possessing a distinguished body, [remains] in a solitary place.

In a place free from disturbances, having assumed the Siddha or other postures, one should pierce the channel of liberation (*kaivalyanāḍī*) through the practice of non-conceptual yoga (*nirvikalpakayoga*). There, by means of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it is ascertained that "only the Self remains";
thus, one should attain *vikalebarakaivalya* (liberation with the physical body). This is the implied meaning. The word "tu" (but/however) serves to emphasize this point.
The two words "iti" and "upaniṣad" signify the completion of the *Yogatattvopaniṣad*.
This very clear commentary on the *Yogatattva* has been written by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The Yogatattvavivaraṇa consists of two hundred and sixty [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Yogatattva Upaniṣad, constituting the forty-first [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Śrīmad Īśa.
